title: The Broken Game
tagline: Four bugs. One broken game. You're the bug detectives.
objectives: I can read someone else's code and work out what it's supposed to do.
I can find a bug by testing, predicting and checking — not guessing randomly.
I can explain in my own words what was wrong and how I fixed it.

config.headline: Every game ever made went on sale with bugs in it.
lines: In 1947, one of the very first computers in the world stopped working. The engineers searched the machine for the fault — and found a real moth stuck inside it. They taped the moth into their logbook and wrote: 'First actual case of bug being found.'

Bugs never went away. Ever since, a BUG has meant a mistake in a program. Every game you have ever played was sold with hundreds of them, found and fixed before the game went on sale. The people who find them are called QA testers. QA is short for Quality Assurance: checking a game really works before players get it. That is a real job — and today it is yours.

In this lesson you will learn to READ code someone else wrote and work out what it is SUPPOSED to do. Then you will find what is actually wrong — by testing, predicting and checking, never by guessing. Those three skills are what this hour is for.

Last night, a games company called OLS GAMES released a new game: Shark Attack. This morning the players' reviews are terrible — four separate bugs got past the old testing team. You are the new QA team. Each complaint a player sends in is called a TICKET, and the tickets are waiting on the board. Save this game.

images.caption: The first computer 'bug' — a real moth, taped into Harvard's logbook, 1947. U.S. Navy photo (public domain).

config.help: This screen is only for reading — it tells you what today's lesson is about. When the writing finishes, press the button at the bottom to start.

config.title: The Case Board
config.intro: Four player tickets, four open cases — each ticket opens a CASE: one bug to find and fix. Play the broken game, read its code, fix ONE thing per case. Then prove the fix by re-playing the game and watching the bug NOT happen. Nobody can check inside Scratch for you: the re-play is your proof, and the case log you write says what you found and what you changed. A case only gets its CASE CLOSED stamp when both are done. Close the training case first; after that, do the cases in any order you like.
config.introSolo: You're on your own today — so you do both jobs: you PLAY the game and you FIX the blocks. Four player tickets, four open cases — each ticket opens a CASE: one bug to find and fix. Play the broken game, read its code, fix ONE thing per case, and prove every fix by re-playing. The re-play is your proof, and the case log you write says what you found and what you changed. A case only gets its CASE CLOSED stamp when both are done. Close the training case first; then do the cases in any order.
config.pairNote: Work as a two-person detective agency with the person beside you: the PLAYER runs the game, reads the ticket out loud and says what they see; the ENGINEER moves the blocks. Swap jobs at every new case — a closed case belongs to both of you.

getgame.intro: A detective examines the REAL broken thing, not a photo of it. Get the broken game open on your own screen:

steps.title: Download the evidence
steps.text: Click the gold button — shark-attack-broken-edition.sb3 drops into your Downloads.

steps.title: Open the Scratch editor
steps.text: Use the second button — scratch.mit.edu opens in a new tab. No login needed, ever. Keep BOTH tabs open: case board here, game there.

steps.title: Load the broken game
steps.text: In Scratch, open the File menu and choose 'Load from your computer'. Pick shark-attack-broken-edition.sb3 from your Downloads, then press OK to replace.

steps.title: Walk the crime scene
steps.text: You should see a Shark, a Fish and a score stuck on 0. Click each sprite in turn and look at its scripts. Every sprite carries its OWN scripts, and they are never shared — that is why a bug can hide on one sprite while everything else looks fine. Most of the bugs are hiding in there — but not all of them: one case will take you somewhere new.

getgame.confirm: The broken game is open in Scratch and I can see its code

handbook.title: Reading Someone Else's Code
handbook.fallback: If the film won't load, don't worry — your teacher's demonstration covers everything it shows, and the cards on this screen walk you through the rest.

chapters.label: Load the game & read its code
Hat blocks: what starts a script

cases.name: The Frozen Shark
cases.ticket: The shark won't swim RIGHT. Left, up, down — all fine. Right? Nothing. My shark just stares at the wall while the fish laugh at it. One star.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag to start the game, then press the RIGHT arrow and count what happens. Now try the other three arrows. The player isn't making it up.
cases.look: Open the Shark's scripts and compare them with each other. Working code is your best evidence: what does every WORKING arrow script start with that the broken one is missing?
cases.logHint: The right-arrow script had no… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag, then fly a full lap: RIGHT along the bottom, UP the far wall, LEFT across the top, DOWN back home. All four arrows, no shortcuts.
cases.replayConfirm: Full lap flown — all four arrows work

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. Which arrows work? Which ONE doesn't? That tells you exactly which script to stare at.
clue.consult: Consult another agency that has CLOSED Case 01 — one question, detective to detective. (Your teacher also solved this one at the front.)
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies on shift — if the ticket re-read didn't crack it, go straight to HQ's clue.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the SHARK. Put the four arrow-key scripts side by side and look at the very TOP of each.

mechanicSteps: The block at the very top of a stack is called a HAT BLOCK — it is what starts a script running. A stack with no hat block never runs at all.
Click Events (the yellow group) and find 'when space key pressed'.
Drag it until it sits ON TOP of the broken stack — a white shadow-line shows when it is about to snap on.
Click its little dropdown and pick the key you need.

cases.name: The Broken Scoreboard
cases.ticket: I ate SO many fish and the score just sits on 0. I can literally HEAR the bite happen. This game is eating my points as well as the fish.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag and eat a fish. Listen for the bite… then look at the score. Eat another one. Still 0?
cases.look: Find the exact moment a fish gets eaten and read that script block by block, OUT LOUD. Every block will sound right — until you reach the one number that is wrong.
cases.logHint: The change-score block said… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag and eat THREE fish, watching the score climb 1, 2, 3. Right once could be luck — right three times is proof.
cases.replayConfirm: Three catches, three points — the scoreboard tells the truth

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The bite HAPPENS — the sound plays, the fish vanishes. So the eaten moment works. What's the one thing that doesn't move?
clue.consult: Consult an agency that has CLOSED Case 02 — one question only, detective to detective. Nobody near you has closed it yet? Then go straight to HQ.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies on shift — if the ticket re-read didn't crack it, go straight to HQ's clue.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the FISH, in the script that starts 'when I start as a clone'.

cases.name: The Vanishing Fish
cases.ticket: One fish. ONE. I ate it in ten seconds flat and then swam round an empty ocean for the rest of my life. Where did everybody GO??
cases.symptom: Click the green flag, eat the first fish, then keep playing for a slow count of ten. Watch the water for new fish the whole time.
cases.look: One script's entire job is making new fish. Find it and read it top to bottom: exactly how many times does it actually make one?
cases.logHint: The fish-maker script only ran… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag and play for twenty full seconds. Fish should KEEP arriving the whole time — count at least five new fish before you tick the stamp.
cases.replayConfirm: Fish kept coming the whole time

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The FIRST fish was fine — it swam, it got eaten. It is everything AFTER that first fish the player never sees. So which script's whole job is making fish?
clue.consult: Ask an agency that has CLOSED Case 03 — one question, and make it a good one. If you are the first in the room to reach it, go straight to HQ instead.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies on shift — if the ticket re-read didn't crack it, go straight to HQ's clue.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the FISH, in the script under 'when green flag clicked' (not the clone one).

mechanicSteps: Drag the blocks you want to repeat OUT onto an empty space first.
Drop a forever block under the hat block.
Drag your blocks back INSIDE the forever block's mouth — Scratch shows a white shadow-line when they are about to land inside.

cases.name: The White Void
cases.ticket: Every single time I press the green flag the sea DISAPPEARS. White screen, fish swimming in nothing, then the ocean strolls in a second late. It looks so broken I stopped playing.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag and watch ONLY the very first second. Now click it again. And again. Same wrongness every time?
cases.look: This one is not on a sprite at all — it is on the STAGE (click the Stage panel on the far right, beside the sprite list). Read its script IN ORDER, top to bottom, and at every single block ask: what is the player seeing RIGHT NOW?
cases.logHint: The script switched to… before… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag three times in a row. The ocean must be on screen from the very first instant, every single time.

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The sea is not missing — it 'strolls in a second late'. So it does arrive. Watch the very first second again and say exactly what you see, in order.
clue.consult: Consult an agency that has CLOSED Case 04 — one question, detective to detective. First one here? Take HQ's clue, no shame in it.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies on shift — if the ticket re-read didn't crack it, go straight to HQ's clue.
clue.hq: Not a sprite at all — open the STAGE's scripts (click the Stage panel, bottom-right, beside the sprite list).

stretchCase.name: The Jellyfish Job
stretchCase.ticket: Five stars, best shark game on the site — but NOTHING can hurt you! Where's the danger? Add something to dodge and it's perfect.
stretchCase.job: Add a Jellyfish from Scratch's sprite library (Choose a Sprite, then search 'Jellyfish'). Build it with the starter blocks below: it drifts to a new spot every couple of seconds, and if the Shark ever touches it, the whole game stops. That 'if touching' block is next lesson's superpower — think of this as a sneak preview. Finished the jellyfish and still hungry? Add ONE more twist of your own design — a second danger, a speed-up, a power-up — and name it in your release note.
stretchCase.test: Click the green flag and dodge the jellyfish for twenty seconds… then swim into it ON PURPOSE. The game should freeze the instant you touch it.
stretchCase.confirm: Danger installed — touching the jellyfish ends the game
stretchCase.ask: One line for the release notes: what did you add, and what does it do to the player?
stretchCase.notePlaceholder: I added a jellyfish that... so now the player...

config.stretchNudge: Your fixed game has gone back to the players — but one five-star request is still pinned to the board. Take the job, or finish for today?

rc.title: The whole-game check
rc.text: Four fixes, one game — and bugs love to hide behind each other. Before the game goes back to the players, QA plays the WHOLE game like a real player: one full minute, from the green flag to the end. Watch all four fixes holding at once:
watch: All four arrows — fly a full lap.
Eat at least five fish — the score counts every single one.
Fish keep arriving for the whole minute.
Restart twice — the ocean is there from the first instant, every time.
rc.confirm: Full sixty-second run — every fix held
rc.ask: Only one number proves you actually ran it: how many fish did you catch in the full run?

ship.intro: When a games company sends a finished game out to its players, they call it SHIPPING the game. A fix only counts once the fixed game is saved somewhere safe — so ship tonight's game to your Drive:

steps.title: Save the fixed game
steps.text: In Scratch, open the File menu and choose 'Save to your computer'. The .sb3 lands in Downloads — that file IS your fixed game.

steps.title: Vault it
steps.text: Open drive.google.com, click into School, then DT Work, and drag the .sb3 in. The same folder as your micro:bit programs.

steps.title: Run the check
steps.text: The website looks in your Drive for a freshly-saved .sb3 — then the players get their game back.

config.boardTip: Lost your game? Nothing is broken — reload scratch.mit.edu, then File → Load from your computer, and pick the .sb3 again.
config.help: The board is your home screen: pins for the film, the broken game, the four cases and the release desk, where you send the fixed game back. Start with Evidence Intake — that gets the broken game open in Scratch — then the TRAINING case. Inside a case: see it happen, read the code, fix ONE thing, write your log, then re-play to prove it. Chapter 3 of the film is the one worth re-watching while you work. Stuck on a case? Its clue routine is on the card, and re-reading the ticket costs you nothing.

config.intro: Two questions about today before you go — and these ARE marked: your teacher sees your answers. Think like a detective, not a guesser.

items.stem: A sprite's script never runs when the green flag is clicked. What's the MOST likely reason?
options: There's no green-flag hat block on that script
The code is at the bottom of the workspace

items.stem: Your partner says: 'Fixed it! I saw one fish get eaten and the score moved.' What does a real QA tester do next?
options: Stamp it CASE CLOSED — it worked once
Re-play it and watch the fix work at least three times before closing the case
Delete the whole script and rebuild it, just to be safe
Add a few extra blocks so it definitely works

config.help: Two marked questions, answered on your own. You find out how you did at the end, after the last screen.

config.intro: Last one. You get five real blocks, and the sentence below describes the game's opening second. Click the blocks into the order the sentence describes — you have spent the whole hour learning why order matters.

item.prompt: When the flag is clicked, the sprite gets into position without the player seeing it move, then appears in the middle of the screen and animates by changing costume forever.

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
config.doneText: Correct — that program does exactly what the card asked.
